title: Unsupervised transfer learning for anomaly detection: Application to complementary operating condition transfer
authors: Michau, Gabriel; Fink, Olga
verified_from: Crossref metadata; KBS abstract (OpenAlex); full text of arXiv:2008.07815v2 (24 Nov 2020 preprint of the same article) saved as raw2/michau2021_arxiv.pdf. Quotes are from the arXiv v2 text; wording of the KBS version not checked line-by-line.
supporting_quote: For each of the five operating modes, (1) take-off, (2) high-altitude cruising, (3) descent, [...] For the target, however, only the data from the second operating mode, high-altitude cruising, in the healthy condition, are available at training time. [...] HELM trained solely on samples from the second operating mode of the target detects all other operating modes as anomalous, which leads to 100% FPR and thus a BA of 50%. [...] Here, this descriptor is 1.2 times the 99.5th percentile [...] we believe FPR and TPR need to be jointly evaluated, FPR to assess whether the rate of false alarms is acceptable and TPR to decide whether the model is worth implementing.
exact_claim_supported: On AGTF30-simulated turbofan flight data split into five flight operating modes (take-off/ascent, high-altitude cruise, descent, lower cruise, landing), a one-class detector whose threshold is set from healthy data of the cruise mode only yields near-100% false-positive rates on the other modes; FPR is reported per operating mode.
relation_to_our_work: Closest found precedent for per-flight-phase FPR reporting and cross-regime transfer of a calibrated detector on simulated turbofan data. Differs from our study: the source detector never saw the other phases (trivial transfer failure), the remedy is cross-unit domain alignment, and pooled-vs-phase calibration, phase disparity of a pooled threshold, delay and flight-level false flags are not studied.
weakens_novelty: partly - per-operating-mode FPR on flight phases and failure of a single-regime calibration to transfer have been shown on a simulated turbofan; our claims must be framed as calibration with all phases present (pooled vs per-phase) rather than 'first to show phase-dependent FPR'.
strengthens_positioning: yes - independent evidence that FPR is flight-mode dependent in simulated turbofan data and that the authors themselves recommend joint FPR/TPR reporting.
recommendation: keep - most direct aero-engine precedent for cross-regime FPR; cite in introduction and in the transfer-matrix discussion.

title: Aircraft Engine Gas Path Diagnostic Methods: Public Benchmarking Results
authors: Simon, Donald L.; Borguet, Sébastien; Léonard, Olivier; Zhang, Xiaodong (Frank)
venue: Journal of Engineering for Gas Turbines and Power
verified_from: Crossref metadata + journal abstract; full text of the NASA report version (NASA/TM-2013-218082, GT2013-95077; NTRS 20140003941) saved as raw2/simon2014_ntrs.pdf. Quotes are from the NASA TM text.
supporting_quote: The EFS produces engine sensed parameter history data consisting of snapshot measurements collected from each engine, each flight, at takeoff and cruise operating points. [...] Users are not provided the associated ground truth information (i.e., knowledge of fault existence or fault type). Instead, the blind-test-case ground truth information is retained by NASA and users are required to submit their diagnostic assessments to NASA for evaluation. [...] Therefore, in an attempt to maintain a level of uniformity in the applied diagnostic methods, a target false alarm rate of no more than one false alarm per 1000 flights is specified. [...] Detection latency: The average number of flights a fault must persist prior to the first true positive detection by the diagnostic algorithm. [...] However, at this relatively low FPR level, even small changes in FPR can have a large effect on other metric results.
exact_claim_supported: ProDiMES benchmarks aircraft-engine gas-path diagnostics on takeoff/cruise snapshot data with a blind test set whose ground truth is withheld, a common flight-level false-alarm target (<=1 per 1000 flights), and joint reporting of FPR, TPR and detection latency (flights); the authors note that small FPR differences strongly affect the other metrics.
relation_to_our_work: Precedent for (i) a withheld-ground-truth (blind) evaluation, (ii) fixing a flight-level false-alarm budget before comparing detection metrics, and (iii) reporting detection latency jointly with FPR, all for aircraft engines. It uses per-flight snapshots (not full-flight time series); its metrics are partitioned by fault evolution rate and fault magnitude, not by operating point; and the blind test is a benchmark-owner hold-out rather than a discovery->freeze->confirmation protocol by the same analyst.
weakens_novelty: partly - joint FPR/latency evaluation under a fixed flight-level false-alarm target and blind held-out testing already exist in aero-engine diagnostics; our novelty must rest on phase-conditional calibration and the pairing with realized healthy-flight false-flag rates on full-flight data.
strengthens_positioning: yes - authoritative aero-engine precedent that false-alarm rate must be matched before comparing latency/TPR, which justifies our pairing of delay with realized false-flag rate.
recommendation: keep - cite when motivating delay reported together with realized false-flag rate and the blind/frozen confirmation logic.

title: Automatic alarm setup using extreme value theory
authors: Toshkova, Daniela; Asher, Matthew; Hutchinson, Paul; Lieven, Nicholas
verified_from: Crossref metadata; abstract read via Semantic Scholar API (raw/10.1016_j.ymssp.2019.106417.s2.json) and identical abstract on the University of Bristol research portal. Full text not read (ScienceDirect blocked).
supporting_quote: In order to avoid triggering false alarms, the individual operational conditions are identified using unsupervised learning system and the threshold levels are set for each condition indicator. [...] Warning and alarm thresholds are determined by applying Generalised Extreme Value (GEV) theory to an established baseline for each operational condition. [...] The results show that determining alert and alarm thresholds alongside the relevant operational conditions provides a more robust indication of the machine components health state compared to using only uniform threshold levels.
exact_claim_supported: MSSP precedent for operational-condition-specific warning/alarm thresholds (GEV per identified operating condition) compared with uniform thresholds, motivated by false-alarm avoidance, on power-plant rotating machinery.
relation_to_our_work: Direct precedent for our phase-conditioned arm C (per-condition thresholds) inside MSSP. The abstract does not report per-condition healthy FPR, cross-condition transfer, or detection delay (full text not read, so absence cannot be confirmed).
weakens_novelty: partly - condition-specific thresholds versus a uniform threshold are not new in MSSP; our contribution cannot be 'proposing per-regime thresholds'.
strengthens_positioning: yes - shows MSSP readership already accepts condition-wise thresholding; our study adds a quantitative audit of what a pooled threshold does per phase and of cross-phase transfer.
recommendation: keep - must be cited (same journal, closest methodological precedent for arm C).

title: Flight-State-Driven Threshold Optimization Framework for Rotorcraft HUMS
authors: Lee, Gyeong Jun; Park, Do Ye; Jeong, Seon Ho; Kim, Jeong Ho
verified_from: Crossref metadata + Crossref abstract (raw/10.3390_aerospace12121110.crossref.json). Full text not read (MDPI blocked automated access).
supporting_quote: Conventional thresholding methods for rotorcraft Health and Usage Monitoring Systems (HUMS) often neglect flight-condition variability, resulting in frequent false alarms. [...] Quantitative results show that the framework significantly reduces the Background Alarm Rate (BAR) to approximately 0.030 compared to the baseline of 0.202, while maintaining a high In-window Alarm Concentration (IAC) comparable to conventional methods.
exact_claim_supported: In in-service rotorcraft HUMS data, thresholds that ignore flight-condition variability cause frequent false alarms; flight-state-aware threshold re-estimation lowered the Background Alarm Rate (0.202 to about 0.030) while maintaining an In-window Alarm Concentration comparable to conventional methods.
relation_to_our_work: Closest aviation analog to our P-vs-C/C' comparison: flight-condition-aware thresholds evaluated jointly on a Background Alarm Rate and an In-window Alarm Concentration (a false-alarm burden metric paired with an alarm-usefulness metric). Differs: vibration CIs on rotorcraft, no simulated benchmark, no frozen protocol; abstract gives no per-flight-state FPR or detection delay.
weakens_novelty: partly - the idea that flight-condition-agnostic thresholds inflate false alarms, and that flight-state-aware thresholds reduce background alarms, is published for HUMS.
strengthens_positioning: yes - independent real-fleet evidence that flight condition drives false alarms; supports external relevance of our simulated result.
recommendation: keep - cite as the closest aviation practice precedent; note that it reports alarm burden, not phase-conditional FPR.

title: Handling Domain Shifts for Anomalous Sound Detection: A Review of DCASE-Related Work

supporting_quote: Furthermore, the optimal decision thresholds for separating the scores belonging to the normal and anomalous data of different data domains differ substantially, which significantly decreases performance when using only a single threshold for both domains. exact_claim_supported: In machine-condition anomalous sound detection, normal-score distributions differ across operating/recording domains, so a single decision threshold shared across domains degrades performance.
relation_to_our_work: Cross-field statement of the same mechanism as our pooled-threshold phase disparity (domain = operating condition). Evaluation there is AUC/pAUC-based rather than healthy FPR per domain; no aero-engine data.

recommendation: keep - cite (with Dohi 2022) as cross-domain evidence that one threshold across operating domains is problematic.

title: Conformal Prediction Under Covariate Shift
authors: Tibshirani, Ryan J.; Foygel Barber, Rina; Candès, Emmanuel J.; Ramdas, Aaditya

exact_claim_supported: Calibration can be transported across covariate shift by likelihood-ratio weighting, provided the ratio is known or estimable.

strengthens_positioning: yes - lets us state the pooled-FPR result as a covariate-shift (phase-mix) issue in established terms.
recommendation: keep - cite in the discussion of calibration-set composition and transportability.
